lessons.title: Segments and identity
lessons.subtitle: An insect body is a row of pieces, and each piece gets its own job.
body: Look at an ant, a fly or a beetle and you will see a body made of a row of pieces. Each piece is called a segment. The row has three big sections: the head at the front, the thorax in the middle, and the abdomen at the back.

Each segment gets an identity. Identity is an instruction that says what the segment will grow. One segment might grow an antenna, another a jaw, another a leg, and another a wing. Some grow nothing at all.

In this lab the body has 18 segments: five in the head (An, Ic, Mn, Mx, Lb), three in the thorax (T1, T2, T3) and ten in the abdomen (A1 to A10). Special genes called Hox genes decide each identity. You will meet them in the next lesson.
lessons.look_for: Only T1, the first thorax segment, changes. It gets the identity of T2: its foreleg turns into a midleg, and the model also grows a wing on it. Same segment, new instruction, new body parts.

quiz.q: What does a segment's identity decide?
options: How many segments the insect has
Which food the insect likes best
What body parts that segment grows
How fast the insect grows up
quiz.explain: Identity is the instruction that tells a segment what to grow, such as an antenna, a leg or a wing.

lessons.title: Eight genes, in order
lessons.subtitle: The genes that set identity line up in the same order as the body they build.
body: A gene is a piece of DNA that holds one instruction. Hox genes are a small team of genes that tell each segment who it is. Insects in this lab have eight: lab, pb, Dfd, Scr, Antp, Ubx, abd-A and Abd-B.

Here is the surprise. The eight genes sit in a row on a chromosome, which is a long strand of DNA, and their order roughly matches the order of the body parts they control. lab works near the front of the head. Abd-B works at the tail end. This match is called colinearity.
The lab uses simplified zones for each gene. For example, lab works in the Ic segment of the head, Dfd in the jaw segments, and Abd-B in A8 to A10.
lessons.look_for: Only Mn, the jaw (mandible) segment, changes. Its small jaw lobe disappears and nothing grows there. Every other segment stays the same.

quiz.q: What does colinearity mean for Hox genes?
options: Gene order on the chromosome matches body order
All eight genes work in every segment
Every Hox gene makes the same protein
The genes only work in the abdomen
quiz.explain: Colinearity means the genes sit on the chromosome in roughly the same front-to-back order as the body parts they control.

lessons.title: The back gene usually wins
lessons.subtitle: When two genes are on in one segment, the one nearer the tail decides.
body: Sometimes two Hox genes are switched on in the same segment. Which one is in charge? Usually the one closer to the back. Scientists call this posterior prevalence, and posterior just means toward the back, or tail end.
Picture two bosses giving different orders. The boss who works further back gets obeyed. In the order of the genes, Ubx comes after Antp, so Ubx wins when both are on.
There are a few exceptions. In this lab, Scr beats Antp even though Antp sits further back. So the rule is a good guide, not a law of nature.
lessons.look_for: Only T2 changes. Antp is already on there, but Ubx is switched on too and wins. T2 takes the identity of T3: its midleg becomes a hindleg, and its wing becomes a haltere, a small balancing knob. Turn on Scientist mode in the Lab to see its label: Documented.

quiz.q: Ubx and Antp are both on in T2. Which one decides what T2 grows?
options: Antp, because it was there first
Neither one, so T2 grows nothing
Both equally, so T2 grows half a wing
Ubx, because it is further back
quiz.explain: The gene further back wins. Ubx gives T3 identity, so the wing becomes a haltere.

lessons.title: Turn a gene off: four wings
lessons.subtitle: Switch off one gene and a fly grows a second pair of wings.
body: A knockout means switching a gene off to see what it was doing. Fruit flies normally have two wings. Behind them sit two tiny knobs called halteres, which help the fly balance in the air. Halteres grow on T3, and Ubx is the gene that tells T3 to make them.

Turn Ubx off and T3 loses its instruction. It then follows the next gene in line, Antp, which means T2 identity. T2 is the segment that grows wings, so the halteres become wings. The fly ends up with four. Real four-winged flies have Ubx switched off in T3, which is what the Lab does here.
Scientist Ed Lewis studied flies like this, called bithorax mutants, and shared the 1995 Nobel Prize for his work on how genes control body plans.
lessons.look_for: Only T3 changes to T2: the hindleg becomes a midleg and the haltere becomes a wing. Count them: four wings. Turn on Scientist mode to see its label: Documented.

quiz.q: What happens to the halteres when Ubx is switched off in a fly?
options: They disappear and leave a gap
They become a second pair of wings
They turn into antennae
They turn into jaws
quiz.explain: Without Ubx, T3 copies T2, so the halteres grow as wings and the fly has four.

lessons.title: Turn a gene on: legs on the head
lessons.subtitle: Switch a gene on in the wrong place and an antenna becomes a leg.
body: The opposite of a knockout is switching a gene on where it is normally off. Antp works in the thorax, where the legs grow. It is normally silent in the antenna segment, called An.
Switch Antp on in An and that segment follows T2 identity. It grows a leg where the antenna should be. Scientists have found real fruit flies with this change. They are called Antennapedia flies.
Notice what Antp did not do. It did not build a leg by itself. It only told the segment which set of instructions to run, and the segment did the building.
lessons.look_for: Only An, the antenna segment at the very front of the head, changes. It takes T2 identity, and the antenna becomes a midleg. Turn on Scientist mode in the Lab to see its label: Documented.

quiz.q: Why does Antp in the antenna segment make a leg?
options: It copies finished legs from the thorax
It deletes every gene in the head
It tells the segment to run the leg program
It makes the whole head bigger
quiz.explain: Hox genes tell a segment which program to run. Antp gives T2 identity, so the segment builds a leg.

lessons.title: Same gene, different insects
lessons.subtitle: The same change makes a different result in a beetle than in a fly.
body: Insects share Hox genes, but they use them on different body parts. A fly has wings on T2 and halteres on T3. A beetle has hard wing covers called elytra on T2 and soft flying wings on T3.
Now switch Ubx off. In both insects, T3 copies T2. In the fly, a haltere becomes a wing. In the beetle, a flying wing becomes a hard cover.
So one gene change can give two different results. Each insect has its own version of T2, and T3 copies whichever version it has.
lessons.look_for: In the beetle, only T3 changes to T2: the hindleg becomes a midleg and the flying wing becomes an elytron (a hard wing case). Now the beetle has four hard wing cases. Compare with the fly in lesson 4.

quiz.q: What happens to a beetle's flying wings when Ubx is switched off?
options: They become hard wing covers
They turn into tiny halteres
They turn into extra antennae
They vanish and leave nothing
quiz.explain: T3 copies T2. A beetle's T2 wings are hard covers called elytra, so the flying wings become elytra.

lessons.title: The head's gene teams
lessons.subtitle: In the head, genes work in pairs, and one gene can do different jobs.
body: Head segments are not built by one gene each. They use combinations of Hox genes. The gene pb is a good example, because its job changes depending on its partner.
With Dfd, pb helps make a maxilla, a jaw part with a small feeler called a palp. With Scr, pb helps make the labium, the insect's lower lip.

Switch pb off and the labium loses its partner. Scr is left alone, and it makes a foreleg instead. Real pb mutants show this. The maxilla change is different. That one is the model's prediction, and no experiment in the lab's records matches it.
lessons.look_for: Two head segments change. Lb, the labium, becomes T1: the fly's sponge-like mouth part turns into a foreleg, which real experiments show. Mx, the maxilla, becomes Mn, a jaw: the palp shrinks to a tiny lobe, which is only the model's prediction. Scientist mode shows these labels.

quiz.q: What does the labium grow when a fly has no pb?
options: A pair of extra wings
A maxillary palp
An antenna
A foreleg
quiz.explain: Without pb, Scr works alone and gives T1 identity, so the labium becomes a foreleg. Real pb mutants do this.

lessons.title: Reading the evidence labels
lessons.subtitle: Not every prediction is equally proven. The labels tell you how sure we are.
body: Each change in the lab carries a label. Documented means a published experiment matches the gene, the change and the result. Model extrapolation means the lab's rules predict it, but no matching experiment is in its records. Published result differs means an experiment found something other than what the rules predict. In the Lab, turn on Scientist mode to see these labels.
A model is a simple copy of something real, used to make predictions. This one is simplified on purpose. Real genes work in big networks, with timing and helpers that the lab leaves out.
So treat the lab as a question generator. It suggests what to test, and experiments decide what is true.
lessons.look_for: Only T2 changes. The model says it loses its leg and its wing, because abd-A wins over the other genes. Turn on Scientist mode and the label says Published result differs: a real experiment turned the wing into a haltere instead. The simple rule misses what really happens, and the label warns you.

quiz.q: What does Model extrapolation tell you?
options: A published study proved it
Experiments found a different result
It is sure to be true in real insects
The rules predict it, but no matching experiment is recorded
quiz.explain: It marks a prediction from the lab's simplified rules that has no matching experiment in its records. It is an idea to test.
